title: Spacing out study sessions beats cramming, even for equal total time
body: The spacing effect, first documented by Hermann Ebbinghaus in 1885, is one of the most robust findings in memory research: material reviewed across several separate sessions is remembered much longer than the same amount of study packed into one. A likely reason is that each gap allows a little forgetting, and the effort of pulling the memory back up strengthens it more than an easy repeat would.

slides.heading: The forgetting curve
slides.text: Ebbinghaus memorised lists of nonsense syllables like ‘WID’ and ‘ZOF’ and retested himself. He forgot fastest soon after learning, then more slowly.

slides.heading: Each review buys time
slides.text: Every well-timed review makes the memory fade more slowly, so the next review can wait longer. Apps that schedule flashcards this way use spaced repetition.

slides.heading: Test, don’t reread
slides.text: Spacing works best with retrieval practice: trying to recall answers from memory, as with flashcards, beats simply rereading your notes.

slides.question: Which review method works best with spacing?
options: Trying to recall answers from memory
slides.explanation: Spacing works best with retrieval practice, as with flashcards: pulling the answer from memory beats rereading, and each well-timed review makes the memory fade more slowly.
